as_told.title: Mellon and Elizondo bring three Navy videos to the Times

plain: In 2017, the story goes, two former Pentagon insiders got three Navy UFO videos cleared for release and brought them to the New York Times. One was Luis Elizondo, who had run a small Pentagon office that studied unexplained aerial reports. The other was Christopher Mellon, a former deputy assistant secretary of defense for intelligence. Michels tells it himself: after Elizondo tried to brief Defense Secretary Jim Mattis on UFOs and was blocked by "bureaucratic intermediaries," the two "took matters into their own hands." The videos ran with the Times article "Glowing Auras and 'Black Money': The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program," published on 16 December 2017. Michels names them as the Tic Tac video from 2004, showing a white oval object shaped like the mint, and the Go Fast and Gimbal videos from 2015. He says the two men brought them to the journalist Leslie Kean, and that the Pentagon had not admitted they were real before. The lawyer Dan Sheehan adds that the Defense Department's Office of Prepublication and Security Review cleared them, so the release was authorised. The skeptic Michael Shermer tells it differently, as the moment the government said UAP (its word for UFOs) "are real." If it happened as they say, it was the first time the Pentagon's own footage of unexplained craft reached the public.
